titre: Hokusai's Great Wave Is Probably Not a Tsunami
accroche: The wave in the print is usually taken for a tidal wave. Cartwright and Nakamura see instead a storm breaker, a rogue wave.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the popular imagination, Hokusai's *The Great Wave* is a tsunami: a mass of water crashing down on boats, with Mount Fuji, tiny, in the distance. The image is so powerful that people rarely question it. Yet the physics of the ocean says otherwise.

## What the Print Says

The print belongs to the *Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji*. The Metropolitan Museum dates it to 1830-1832 and gives it under its Japanese title, *Kanagawa oki nami ura*, which can be rendered as “Under the Wave off Kanagawa.” The word “tsunami” does not appear. Mount Fuji is painted small, and Capucine Korenberg, of the British Museum, notes that it can be mistaken for another crest of the ocean.

## Two Phenomena That Get Confused

A tsunami is born of a massive displacement of water, an earthquake or an eruption. Out at sea, it is only a long wave a few tens of centimeters in amplitude, which ships do not notice. It becomes destructive only as it nears the coast, when the depth decreases.

A rogue wave (*vague scélérate* in French) is something else: an isolated wave, far taller than those around it, focused in both time and space, on a rough sea. This is what the print shows, according to J. H. E. Cartwright and H. Nakamura, in a 2009 article in *Notes and Records of the Royal Society*. According to the summary given by Dudley and his colleagues in 2013, they see in it a storm breaker about to crash down on the transport boats, which are rowing against the direction of the wave. They place the scene about 3 km from the coast, in Tokyo Bay, and estimate the height at about ten meters, exceptional for those waters.

## A Photograph from 1991

Dudley, Sarano and Dias compare the print to a photograph taken in 1991 from the French research vessel *Astrolabe*, in sub-Antarctic waters: an isolated wave, focused in both dimensions, which breaks in a way very close to what Hokusai drew.

## The Shift

The point is not that Hokusai documented a specific event. The height estimate is an inference drawn from an image, and the authors speak of a reading far more probable than the tsunami one, not a certainty. But it changes how the print is read. A print run, by current estimates, of up to 8,000 impressions readily passes for the image of a catastrophe, when it would instead show a storm sea at its most extreme.

There remains the matter of the height: ten meters is deduced from boats drawn by an artist, which does not amount to a measurement.

repere.texte: A photograph taken in 1991 from the French research vessel Astrolabe, in sub-Antarctic waters, shows a rogue wave whose spatial focusing and breaking resemble those of Hokusai's print.
repere.source: J. M. Dudley, V. Sarano, F. Dias, “On Hokusai's Great wave off Kanagawa: localization, linearity and a rogue wave in sub-Antarctic waters,” Notes and Records of the Royal Society, vol. 67, 2013

carte.punch: Hokusai's Great Wave is probably not a tsunami.
carte.idee: In open sea, a tsunami is only a few tens of centimeters high. Hokusai's wave looks more like a storm rogue wave, about ten meters high according to Cartwright and Nakamura (2009), and like a photo taken in 1991 in the southern ocean.

quiz.question: Why wouldn't a tsunami look like the wave in the print, out at sea?
choix: It becomes tall only as it nears the coast, not offshore
Tsunamis are always smaller than a storm wave
Wind produces tsunamis, just like storm waves
Tsunamis never occur in the Pacific
quiz.explication: A tsunami is born of a massive displacement of water (earthquake, eruption) and grows only as it nears the coast, when the depth decreases. It is not driven by the wind, it can be taller than a storm wave once ashore, and it also strikes the Pacific.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the Metropolitan Museum, which series does Hokusai's print belong to, and around what years was it produced?
choix: *One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji*, around 1849
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Metropolitan Museum dates the print to 1830-1832 and places it in the Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, under its Japanese title Kanagawa oki nami ura.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Cartwright and Nakamura, how far from the coast and at roughly what height do they place the wave in the print?
choix: In open sea, several hundred kilometers from the coast
About 3 km from the coast, at a height of a few centimeters
About 3 km from the coast, at a height of about ten meters
Right at the shoreline, at a height of thirty meters
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Dudley, Sarano and Dias report that Cartwright and Nakamura place the scene about 3 km from the coast in Tokyo Bay, with a height on the order of ten meters, exceptional for those waters.
